summary: Describes the frame format for IPv6 packets over IEEE 802.15.4 networks, how to form link-local and autoconfigured addresses, a simple header compression scheme, and mesh delivery. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Small low-power sensors can speak IPv6 if the messages are shrunk to fit. This note says how to pack them.

questions: how to send ipv6 over ieee 802.15.4
what is the ipv6 mtu on 802.15.4
subtitle: How to squeeze 1280-byte IPv6 packets onto tiny 127-byte IEEE 802.15.4 radio frames.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs links that carry packets of at least 1280 octets, but an IEEE 802.15.4 frame leaves at most 102 octets at the MAC layer, and as few as 81 with link-layer security.
tldr.mechanism: A thin adaptation layer (the LoWPAN encapsulation) adds fragmentation, optional mesh addressing and a simple header compression scheme, and defines how to build interface identifiers and link-local addresses from 802.15.4 addresses.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 can run on low-power radio networks, and a typical link-local packet can shrink its 40-octet IPv6 header to 2 octets. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 6282, RFC 6775, RFC 8025, RFC 8066 and RFC 8931.

today: RFC 4944 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6282, RFC 6775, RFC 8025, RFC 8066 and RFC 8931. It has not been obsoleted, so check those updates alongside this text.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The IEEE 802.15.4 standard targets low-power personal area networks (PANs). RFC 4944 defines the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over such networks, and how to form IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured addresses on top of them.

Because IPv6 expects far larger packets than an 802.15.4 frame can hold, the RFC defines an adaptation layer. It also defines a header compression scheme and the provisions needed to deliver packets across an 802.15.4 mesh. A full specification of mesh routing itself (which routing protocol, how it interacts with neighbor discovery) is explicitly out of scope.

IPv6 packets MUST be carried in 802.15.4 data frames. The RFC recommends asking for link-layer acknowledgements to help recovery. It does not require beacon-enabled mode; in nonbeacon-enabled networks data frames use unslotted CSMA/CA.
sections.eli5: Small battery gadgets talk by radio in tiny messages. This note explains how they can still speak the big, modern internet language, IPv6.

sections.title: Why the Frames Are Too Small
sections.content:
The IPv6 link MTU defined here is 1280 octets. An 802.15.4 physical packet is at most 127 octets (aMaxPHYPacketSize), and with a maximum frame overhead of 25 octets (aMaxFrameOverhead) the largest MAC frame is 102 octets. Link-layer security takes more: 21 octets in the AES-CCM-128 case (9 and 13 for AES-CCM-32 and AES-CCM-64), leaving only 81 octets.

The 40-octet IPv6 header then leaves 41 octets for upper layers. UDP uses 8 of those, leaving 33 octets for application data, before any fragmentation overhead.

The RFC draws two conclusions. First, an adaptation layer for fragmentation and reassembly is needed to meet IPv6's minimum MTU, though most applications are expected to use small payloads that fit in one frame once headers are compressed. Second, header compression is "compelling to the point of almost being unavoidable".
sections.eli5: Imagine posting a long letter through a mail slot only big enough for a postcard. You have to cut the letter into pieces, and it helps a lot to write in short-hand.

sections.title: The LoWPAN Header Stack
sections.content:
Every LoWPAN datagram starts with a stack of encapsulation headers, each beginning with a type. The LoWPAN payload (for example an IPv6 packet) follows. When more than one header is used, they MUST appear in this order: Mesh Addressing, Broadcast, then Fragmentation.

The first bits of a header are its dispatch value. For example 01 000001 means an uncompressed IPv6 header follows, 01 000010 means a LOWPAN_HC1 compressed header, 10 starts a mesh header, and 00 marks a frame that is Not A LoWPAN frame (NALP), which any LoWPAN node discards. Non-LoWPAN protocols that want to coexist should put a byte matching the NALP pattern right after the 802.15.4 header.

The mesh header begins with bits 1 0, then a V bit and an F bit saying whether the originator and final destination addresses are 64-bit (0) or 16-bit short (1) addresses, then a 4-bit Hops Left field. Each forwarder decrements Hops Left, and the packet is not forwarded if it reaches zero. The value 0xF is reserved and signals an 8-bit Deep Hops Left field, allowing hop limits above 14.
sections.eli5: Each message gets labels stuck on the front in a fixed order, like a parcel with a mesh-route sticker, a pieces sticker and then the contents. The first bits of each label say what kind of label it is.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly
sections.content:
If an IPv6 datagram does not fit in one frame it SHALL be split into link fragments. The fragment offset counts in units of 8 octets, so every fragment except the last MUST be a multiple of eight bytes long. The first fragment carries a header with an 11-bit datagram_size and a 16-bit datagram_tag. Later fragments add an 8-bit datagram_offset.

The size is that of the whole IP packet before link fragmentation, which for IPv6 is 40 octets more than the Payload Length. The tag is the same for all fragments of one datagram, is incremented for each new fragmented datagram and wraps from 65535 to zero.

A receiver identifies fragments of one datagram by the source and destination 802.15.4 addresses (or the mesh originator and final destination), plus datagram_size and datagram_tag. It reassembles into a buffer sized from datagram_size. If an overlapping fragment differs in size or offset, the accumulated fragments are discarded. On an 802.15.4 disassociation event, partial reassemblies MUST be dropped. The reassembly timer MUST be set to a maximum of 60 seconds.
sections.eli5: A big picture is cut into puzzle pieces. Each piece says which puzzle it belongs to and where it fits. If the missing pieces do not show up in time, the receiver throws the half-built puzzle away.

sections.title: Addresses, Link-Local and Multicast
sections.content:
802.15.4 devices have 64-bit extended addresses (EUI-64) and may also get 16-bit short addresses from the PAN coordinator. The RFC warns that short addresses are transient: they last only as long as the association, and a single coordinator is a scalability limit and single point of failure. A PAN maps to one IPv6 link.

The interface identifier is normally built from the EUI-64 as in "IPv6 over Ethernet" (RFC 2464). For short addresses, a pseudo 48-bit address is formed from 16 zero bits, the 16-bit PAN ID (or 16 zero bits if unknown) and the 16-bit short address, and the U/L bit is set to zero. All-zero addresses MUST NOT be used. Autoconfigured prefixes MUST be 64 bits long, and the link-local address is the interface identifier appended to FE80::/64.

802.15.4 has no native multicast, so IPv6 multicast MUST be sent as link-layer broadcast to the 16-bit address 0xffff with the PAN's own PAN ID. Inside a mesh, an IPv6 multicast destination maps to a 16-bit address of the form 100 followed by the last 5 bits of DST[15] and all of DST[16]. Short addresses starting with bit 0 are unicast, and the RFC creates IANA registries for the dispatch values and the short address format.
sections.eli5: Every gadget has a long serial number and maybe a short nickname. The IPv6 name is built from one of them. To shout to everybody, the gadget just broadcasts to the whole group of radios.

sections.title: Header Compression (HC1 and HC_UDP)
sections.content:
Compression here is deliberately simple. It keeps no per-flow state and relies on what devices in the same 6LoWPAN already share. The LOWPAN_HC1 encoding assumes the common case: version is IPv6, both addresses are link-local, interface identifiers can be inferred from the link-layer addresses, the length can be inferred from the frame or datagram_size, Traffic Class and Flow Label are zero, and Next Header is UDP, ICMP or TCP. Only the 8-bit Hop Limit must always be sent, so the 40-octet header can shrink to 2 octets (1 for HC1, 1 for Hop Limit).

The 8-bit HC1 encoding uses two bits each for the source and destination address (prefix carried in-line or compressed, interface identifier carried in-line or elided), one bit for Traffic Class and Flow Label, two bits for Next Header (not compressed, UDP, ICMP, TCP) and one bit saying an HC2 encoding follows.

For UDP, the HC_UDP encoding can compress each port to 4 bits as 61616 (0xF0B0) plus a short value, and can drop the length, which is derived from the IPv6 Payload Length. The checksum is always carried in full. The UDP header can shrink to 4 octets from 8. Compressed headers are padded with zero bits to an octet boundary.
sections.eli5: If everyone in a club already knows the club's address, you do not need to write it on every note. You just tick a box that says same as usual, and only write what is different.

sections.title: Delivery Across a Mesh
sections.content:
802.15.4 does not itself define mesh routing, so the RFC adds a way to carry end-to-end link-layer addresses. A node that cannot reach the destination directly includes a Mesh Addressing header with the Originator address set to itself and the Final Destination set to the packet's ultimate target, then sends the frame to a default forwarder.

A receiving node reads the Final Destination. If it is the destination, it consumes the packet. Otherwise it decrements Hops Left, discards the packet if it reaches zero, looks up the next hop in its link-layer routing table, and retransmits with itself as the 802.15.4 source. Only Full Function Devices (FFDs) are expected to route; Reduced Function Devices (RFDs) use an FFD as their forwarder, like a host with a default router.

A broadcast header (dispatch LOWPAN_BC0) adds an 8-bit sequence number that the originator increments for each new mesh broadcast or multicast, to detect duplicates. How broadcast and routing are handled in detail is out of scope. Appendix A explains the alternative of using IP addresses for mesh delivery, which was rejected partly because fragments arriving out of order would force nodes to buffer until the first fragment shows up.
sections.eli5: Pass-the-parcel: each kid knows the final person it is for, hands it to a neighbour who is closer, and the parcel is thrown away if it has been passed too many times.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Interface identifiers derived from EUI-64 addresses aim to preserve global uniqueness, but there is no protection from duplication through accident or forgery. Neighbor Discovery on 802.15.4 links may face the threats described in RFC 3756, and mesh routing adds ad hoc routing threats.

802.15.4 offers link-layer security using AES modes, but it does not specify key management. The RFC urges users to use link-layer security where practical, and notes that simple devices may rely heavily on it. Full Function Devices that talk to off-link IPv6 peers are expected to secure end-to-end communication with the usual mechanisms such as IPsec or TLS.
sections.eli5: The radio can lock its messages, but nobody said who hands out the keys. So the people who build a network must plan that part themselves.

items.label: NALP
items.desc: Not a LoWPAN frame; LoWPAN nodes discard it.

fields.name: datagram_size
fields.desc: Size of the whole IP packet before link-layer fragmentation.

fields.name: datagram_tag
fields.desc: Same for all fragments of one datagram; incremented per fragmented datagram.

items.label: Source address
items.desc: 00 PI,II; 01 PI,IC; 10 PC,II; 11 PC,IC (prefix carried or compressed; interface identifier carried or elided).

items.label: Destination address
items.desc: Same four combinations as the source address.

items.label: Traffic Class and Flow Label
items.desc: 1 means both are zero; 0 means they are sent in full.

items.label: Next Header
items.desc: 00 sent in full; 01 UDP; 10 ICMP; 11 TCP.

items.label: HC2 encoding
items.desc: 1 means more compression bits (such as HC_UDP) follow.
